hero.title: The quiz to find out what dog you two should get
hero.titleHighlight: what dog you two should get
hero.description: You both want a dog, but maybe not the same one? You each answer twelve questions about your life together, and the quiz gives you the dog that suits you both, with its photo.
hero.subtitle: 12 questions • 3 minutes each • on one phone

section1.title: How the quiz works
section1.p1: This quiz is here to find the dog that would suit you as a couple, and not just one of you. It asks twelve very simple questions about the life you'd have with it: where you live, what you do on a Sunday morning, how long it would be left alone, whether dog hair on the sofa bothers you, etc.
section1.p2: For example, for the question “Its size:”, you can choose between “small, it fits on your lap”, “medium, you can still carry it”, “big, a proper dog” and “huge, almost a pony”. If you answer “small” and your other half answers “huge”, the quiz takes that into account: it adds up your two sets of answers and keeps the dog with the best score for the two of you.
section1.p3: Together, the first one answers the twelve questions, passes the phone, and the second one answers without seeing what the other chose. At the end, you get the couple's dog with its photo, the dog each of you would have got on your own, and the list of questions where you didn't give the same answer. That's often where the conversation starts!
section1.p4: You can also take it on your own, answering for the two of you. But it's a lot more fun to find out what the other one answered.

section2.title: The twelve dogs in the quiz
section2.intro: The quiz can land on twelve results: ten of the best-known breeds, the rescue dog, and one last result for couples who aren't ready yet. Here's who each one suits best.

section3.title: Choosing a dog as a couple: what to ask yourselves
section3.intro: A dog lives ten to fifteen years. It's a decision you make together, and there are four subjects it's better to agree on before you go and see one.
section3.sub1Title: Who looks after it, and when?
section3.sub1Text: This is the question that causes the most arguments. A dog goes out three times a day, every day, including Sunday mornings in the rain. Before you adopt, agree on who does what at home: the morning walk, the lunchtime visit, the vet, and the broken nights if it's a puppy.
section3.sub2Text: A big sporty dog in a studio, or a very clingy little dog left alone ten hours a day: that goes badly for everyone. Look at your life as it is today, not the one you'd like to have. And if you don't yet agree on where you want to live, start there: a garden changes a lot of things.
section3.sub3Text: It's not just the food. You need to count the vet, the vaccinations, insurance if you take some out, grooming for certain breeds, and someone to look after it when you go away without it. A big dog costs more than a small one, quite simply because it eats more. Do the sums together beforehand, it avoids nasty surprises.
section3.sub4Title: A puppy or an adult, a breeder or a shelter
section3.sub4Text: A puppy is cute, but it also means months of training, short nights and chewed shoes. An adult dog is often already house-trained, and you know its character. In a shelter you'll find dogs of all ages, mixed breeds but pedigree dogs too. If you go through a breeder, go and see the parents and the place where the puppies grow up.

section4.title: What if you don't agree?
section4.p1: The quiz result is a starting point. If one of you dreams of a husky and the other of a dog that fits in a bag, the most interesting part is in the list of your different answers. Look at what you disagree on (size, how long it would be alone, holidays) and talk about it. Most of the time, it comes down to two or three questions, not all of them.
section4.p2: Lots of couples get a dog before having a child. The two have nothing in common, of course, but it already means getting organised together for someone who depends on you, and you soon see how each of you goes about it.
section4.p3: And if one of you doesn't want one at all, don't push. It's better to wait until you both want it than to have a dog only one of you looks after.

section5.title: What you should know about this quiz
section5.p1: This quiz is a game. The descriptions give the most common character of each breed, but every dog is different, and its upbringing matters as much as its breed. To make your choice, go and see breeders, shelters or a vet, and spend time with the dog before you decide.
section5.p2: Nothing is saved: your answers stay on your phone. Only the dog you get is counted, with no name attached, to see which results come up most. The photos of the dogs were created for this page.

seo.faq1A: Twelve results are possible: the golden retriever, the corgi, the French bulldog, the Cavalier King Charles spaniel, the Australian shepherd, the dachshund, the poodle, the Shiba Inu, the Siberian husky, the Bernese mountain dog, the rescue dog, and “a plush dog, for now” for couples who aren't ready yet.
seo.faq2Q: How is the result worked out?
seo.faq2A: Each answer gives points to the dogs that match it. For example, “in a city apartment, with no outdoor space” gives points to the French bulldog and the Cavalier King Charles spaniel, and none to the husky. With two of you, the quiz adds up your two sets of answers, and the dog with the best score becomes the couple's dog.
seo.faq3Q: Can you take the quiz on your own?
seo.faq3A: Yes. Choose “On my own, for the two of us” and answer with the two of you in mind. You'll get a dog, but not the comparison of your answers: for that, there have to be two of you.
seo.faq4Q: What dog for a young couple in an apartment?
seo.faq4A: It mostly depends on how much time you have. In an apartment, the dogs that do best are the ones that don't need to run for hours: the French bulldog, the Cavalier King Charles spaniel, the dachshund or the poodle. The Shiba Inu also works if you're out at work part of the day. An Australian shepherd or a husky, on the other hand, needs space and a lot of exercise.
seo.faq5Q: How do we know if we're ready for a dog?
seo.faq5A: The quiz has a result for that: “a plush dog, for now”. It comes up when your answers say the dog would be alone all day, that you travel a lot, or that you don't both want it as much. If you land on it, look after a friend's dog for a weekend and see how it goes.
